summary:
Christopher Burns opens by disclaiming expertise: he is self-taught and 'hacking' on agent discoverability. He founded Inth and built c15t, an open source consent banner library whose stats he presents: ~3 million npm downloads, ~45% month-on-month growth, ~2,800 production websites. After Y Combinator, his onboarding form's 'how did you hear about us' field spiked on April 13th; LLMs became the single largest inbound channel. He frames the shift via the Collison brothers' Stripe-install anecdote: founders now hand over a prompt, meaning DX primitives are agent-experience primitives.

Burns describes c15t as an iceberg of micro-optimizations, likening the toolkit to Batman's utility belt. He and peers abstracted these into a framework-neutral docs pipeline called 'Lead Type' that ingests MDX and emits agent-facing artifacts.

Practical tactics: (1) Hand-write llms.txt — ~40 good lines beats ~1,000 generated lines. (2) Provide llms-full.txt as a sitemap with one-line descriptions. (3) Serve markdown via three delivery methods: a .md suffix, content negotiation via Accept header, and a `?mode=agent` query parameter. (4) Emerging: Web MCP exposing search/get-page/ask-docs tools. (5) Most important: ship bundled markdown and an AGENTS.md inside the npm package since coding agents read node_modules and stale training data rather than docs sites.

He measures ~50% token savings across models, mentions Cloudflare's and Aura AI's agent-readiness tests, and closes by cautioning the field shifts weekly. Q&A confirms: ship llms.txt first, then llms-full.txt, write them manually, and get creative generating files even on systems without native markdown.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Disclaimer and speaker credentials
sections.summary: Burns warns the talk title may already be obsolete because the field shifts every few days. He emphasizes he is not a researcher and is 'hacking' on agent discoverability. He introduces himself as founder of Inth and creator of c15t.

sections.title: c15t stats and the April 13th LLM inbound spike
sections.summary: Burns presents adoption metrics: ~3 million npm downloads, ~45% month-on-month growth, ~2,800 production websites. The onboarding 'how did you hear about us' field spiked starting April 13th; LLMs became c15t's single largest inbound source.

sections.title: Why DX primitives became agent primitives
sections.summary: Burns references the Collison brothers' Stripe-install anecdote and contrasts it with today's prompt-based install inside Y Combinator. He argues developer-experience primitives and agent-experience primitives are now the same surface.

sections.title: The docs pipeline and framework-neutral tooling
sections.summary: No single tool fixes discoverability. Burns and peers abstracted optimizations into Lead Type — a framework-neutral docs pipeline that ingests MDX and emits all agent-facing artifacts.

sections.title: Hand-written llms.txt and llms-full.txt
sections.summary: Write llms.txt by hand (~40 good lines beats ~1,000 generated lines) and provide an llms-full.txt acting as a sitemap of pages with one-line descriptions, because agents fetch rather than browse.

sections.title: Serving markdown instead of HTML, three ways
sections.summary: Ship markdown instead of HTML via three redundant delivery methods: a .md URL suffix, Next.js content negotiation via Accept header, and a `?mode=agent` query parameter for agents that cannot append headers.

sections.title: Web MCP and asking docs
sections.summary: Emerging tactic: expose MCP tools so an agent can ask the website questions. Lead Type already exposes three tools — search docs, get pages, ask docs.

sections.title: In-package markdown and AGENTS.md
sections.summary: Coding agents rarely visit documentation sites, instead reading the repo and node_modules with stale training data. Ship bundled markdown plus an AGENTS.md inside the npm package itself. Burns measures ~50% token savings across multiple models.

sections.title: Agent-readiness testing and closing caution
sections.summary: Burns mentions Cloudflare's agent-readiness harness and his favorite, Aura AI, which scored c15t at 59. He closes by cautioning that nothing stays perfect and every small increment matters.

sections.title: Q&A — starting point for a plain website
sections.summary: A website agency asks where to start. Burns answers: prioritize a .md file per page. Q&A concludes with the priority order — llms.txt first, llms-full.txt second, write them manually, and get creative generating files even on systems without native markdown to keep token efficiency up.

demonstrations: Running `lead-type generate` on MDX to emit all agent-facing artifacts.
Serving the same content as HTML, .md suffix, Accept-header markdown, and ?mode=agent.
Exposing three Web MCP tools: search docs, get pages, ask docs.
Aura AI agent-readiness test scoring c15t at 59 (declining from a higher score three weeks prior).
limitations: CMSs often lack native markdown export.
Not every agent honors Accept-header content negotiation.
Coding agents largely never visit documentation sites, relying on stale training data and compiled source.
Agent-readiness scores drift week to week; no stable perfection.
Web MCP tooling is described as still very early.
